title: Continuous basis lifts split a topologically finite free quotient
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with a topology making addition, negation and multiplication continuous. Let $M,N$ be $A$-modules with topologies making addition, negation and the scalar actions $A\times M\to M$ and $A\times N\to N$ continuous. Let $I$ be a finite set, possibly empty, and let $(b_i)_{i\in I}$ be an $A$-basis of $N$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module], meaning every $x\in N$ is uniquely $\sum_i a_i b_i$. Assume its coordinate map $\beta:A^I\to N$, $a\mapsto\sum_i a_i b_i$, is a homeomorphism for the product topology on $A^I$. Let $q:M\to N$ be a continuous surjective $A$-linear map. For any choice of lifts $m_i\in M$ with $q(m_i)=b_i$, the formula
$$s(x)=\sum_{i\in I}(\beta^{-1}(x))_i m_i$$
defines a continuous $A$-linear map $s:N\to M$ with $q\circ s=\mathrm{id}_N$ and $s(b_i)=m_i$. In particular such a section exists. For every topological space $Z$, write $C(Z,M)$ and $C(Z,N)$ for continuous maps, with pointwise $C(Z,A)$-module structures. Postcomposition induces a surjective $C(Z,A)$-linear map $q_*:C(Z,M)\to C(Z,N)$ with a $C(Z,A)$-linear right inverse $s_*:f\mapsto s\circ f$. These maps commute with precomposition by every continuous map $Z'\to Z$. The assertion includes $N=0$ and the empty basis.

proof.text: Write $c(x)=\beta^{-1}(x)$ and $c_i(x)=c(x)_i$. By the uniqueness of basis expansions [def-weil-pbc-free-module], $c(x+y)=c(x)+c(y)$ and $c(ax)=a c(x)$: applying $\beta$ to the right sides gives $x+y$ and $ax$, respectively. Likewise $c(0)=0$ and $c(b_j)=e_j$, where $(e_j)_i$ is $1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. These arguments use only the module distributive laws and uniqueness, and work also over the zero ring.

proof.text: Fix any lifts $m_i$ as in the statement and put $s(x)=\sum_{i\in I}c_i(x)m_i$. Substituting the preceding coordinate identities and distributing the finite sums gives $s(x+y)=\sum_i(c_i(x)+c_i(y))m_i=s(x)+s(y)$ and $s(ax)=\sum_i(a c_i(x))m_i=a s(x)$; also $s(0)=0$. Thus this formula defines an $A$-linear map for every prescribed family of lifts.

proof.text: Linearity of $q$ and the prescribed equations $q(m_i)=b_i$ give $q(s(x))=\sum_i c_i(x)q(m_i)=\sum_i c_i(x)b_i=\beta(c(x))=x$. Moreover $s(b_j)=\sum_i(e_j)_i m_i=m_j$. This proves the section identity and the specified values, without choosing any additional lift.

proof.text: Each $c_i$ is continuous, being the composite of the continuous inverse homeomorphism $\beta^{-1}$ with the $i$th product projection. The map $x\mapsto(c_i(x),m_i)$ is continuous into $A\times M$: the inverse image of a basic rectangle $U\times V$ is $c_i^{-1}(U)$ when $m_i\in V$ and is empty otherwise. Composition with the assumed continuous scalar action makes $x\mapsto c_i(x)m_i$ continuous. Induct on the finite set of summands: the empty partial sum is the continuous constant zero map, and adjoining one summand composes the pair of continuous partial-sum and summand maps with continuous addition. Pair continuity is checked on the same basic rectangles by intersecting the two open inverse images. Hence $s$ is continuous.

source.place: Pushing down by the trace, sentence identifying L_0 with the continuous module of the sum lattice: continuous lifting through the sum map; general coordinate lemma extracted by Q46 from the explicit argument of lem-sfb-continuous-lattice-sum; explicit coordinate argument, step 4

proof.text: Surjectivity of $q$ supplies one $m_i\in q^{-1}(b_i)$ for each of the finitely many $i$, so a family of lifts and therefore a section exists. If $I$ is empty, $A^I$ has its single empty tuple and the basis expansion says that every $x\in N$ is the empty sum $0$. The formula is then $s(0)=0$, continuous and linear, and $q(s(0))=0$ is the identity on $N$. No element of an empty family is chosen. The same coordinate calculations cover $N=0$ whenever a basis satisfying the hypotheses is supplied.

proof.text: For any topological space $Z$, the pointwise operations on $C(Z,A)$, $C(Z,M)$ and $C(Z,N)$ are well defined: sums, negatives, products of scalar functions, and products of a scalar function with a module-valued function are obtained by pairing continuous maps and composing with the corresponding assumed continuous operation. Pairing is continuous by the rectangle calculation in the preceding continuity step, and the zero and unit maps are constant. The commutative ring and module identities hold at each $z\in Z$, hence hold as equalities of functions. This gives precisely the stated pointwise $C(Z,A)$-modules.

proof.text: Postcomposition defines $q_*(f)=q\circ f$ and $s_*(g)=s\circ g$ on these continuous maps, since composition preserves continuity. For $a\in C(Z,A)$ and $f,h\in C(Z,M)$, evaluation at $z$ gives $q_*(f+h)(z)=q(f(z))+q(h(z))$ and $q_*(af)(z)=a(z)q(f(z))$; the identical formulas with $s$ prove linearity of $s_*$. Finally $(q_*s_*g)(z)=q(s(g(z)))=g(z)$ for every $z$, so $q_*s_*=\mathrm{id}$ and every $g$ has the continuous lift $s_*g$. These equalities also apply when $Z$ is empty.

proof.text: Let $u:Z^\prime\to Z$ be continuous. Precomposition sends a continuous $f$ to $f\circ u$ and respects pointwise operations, with scalar functions restricted by $a\mapsto a\circ u$. Associativity of composition gives $q\circ(f\circ u)=(q\circ f)\circ u$ and $s\circ(g\circ u)=(s\circ g)\circ u$. Thus both $q_*$ and its chosen right inverse $s_*$ commute with every specified precomposition map.
